title: Ukraine during World War I
summary: During World War I, Ukraine was divided between the Russian and Austro-Hungarian Empires, with significant implications for its population and nationalist movements. The war exacerbated existing tensions and led to widespread suffering among Ukrainians caught in the conflict.

sections.heading: Political Context
paragraphs: At the onset of World War I, [[ukraine|Ukraine]] was not an independent state but was largely incorporated into the Russian Empire, with a western region under Austro-Hungarian control. The borders between these empires were established at the Congress of Vienna in 1815.

In the late 19th century, both the Russian and Austro-Hungarian Empires sought to influence [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] territories amid a rising sense of nationalism. The Russian Empire regarded [[ukrainians|Ukrainians]] as Little Russians and had support from Russophile communities, while Austria-Hungary fostered [[ukrainian-nationalism|Ukrainian nationalism]].

sections.heading: Military Engagements
paragraphs: The Russian military campaign in [[galicia|Galicia]] commenced in August 1914, achieving significant territorial gains against the Austrians. Approximately 3.5 million Ukrainians served in the Imperial Russian Army, while around 250,000 fought for the Austro-Hungarian Army, leading to instances of Ukrainians fighting against each other.

sections.heading: Impact on Civilians
paragraphs: The conflict severely affected Ukrainian civilians, with villages often destroyed during military operations. In Galicia, over 20,000 Ukrainians suspected of supporting Russian interests were detained in Austrian concentration camps.

The retreat of Russian forces in 1915 prompted a mass exodus of approximately 3.5 million civilians fleeing from advancing German and Austro-Hungarian troops. This evacuation led to widespread looting, destruction of infrastructure, and forced deportations, particularly targeting Eastern Orthodox populations.

sections.heading: Post-War Developments
paragraphs: Following the Russian Revolution of 1917, Ukraine experienced intensified conflict as various factions vied for control. Despite attempts to establish independent Ukrainian states in [[kyiv|Kyiv]] and Lemberg, these efforts failed to gain international recognition.

The Treaty of Versailles in 1919 determined the borders of Ukraine, with Galicia and western [[volhynia|Volhynia]] assigned to Poland, [[bukovina|Bukovina]] to Romania, and central and eastern territories to [[soviet-union|the Soviet Union]], leading to a significant loss of Ukrainian aspirations for statehood.
